notes: GMAC guarantee summary judgment; Etridge misrepresentation defence to Part 24 and invoice discounting mechanics are clear.

enrichment.short_title: GMAC summary judgment on Sandhu father-and-son guarantees
key_facts: GMAC Commercial Credit Development Ltd sued Kalvinder and Kewal Singh Sandhu under identical Deeds of Guarantee and Indemnity dated 18 June 1999 given in connection with invoice discounting arrangements with Donnaway Ltd.
GMAC applied for summary judgment under CPR Part 24 on multiple defences raised by the guarantors, including alleged premature demands and misrepresentation.

Kewal Sandhu alleged his son Kalvinder misrepresented the effect of the discounting documentation and that GMAC was put on inquiry under Barclays Bank v O'Brien and Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2).
GMAC had taken no steps to explain the guarantee risks to Kewal or secure independent legal advice for him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judgment on GMAC's Part 24 summary judgment application in guarantee enforcement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: GMAC obtained summary judgment on several defences including the listing point; Part 24 application dismissed in relation to Kewal's Etridge-based misrepresentation defence because he had a real prospect of proving a non-commercial surety relationship.
enrichment.ratio: On a Part 24 application, a guarantor has a real prospect of defending under Lord Nicholls' Etridge principle where he may prove no commercial relationship with the principal debtor and the creditor took no steps to bring home the risks of the guarantee; Etridge may apply to pre-October 2001 transactions where the facts support the developed principle.
legal_issues: Whether GMAC's demands under the guarantees were premature
Whether summary judgment should be granted on listing and other technical defences
Whether Kewal could rely on alleged misrepresentation and Etridge undue influence principles
Whether Kewal had a commercial or non-commercial relationship with Donnaway
index_terms: Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland Plc v Etridge (No 2) [2002] 2 AC 773
Barclays Bank Plc v O'Brien [1994] 1 AC 180

confidence.notes: Core Part 24 and Etridge analysis is explicit. Some invoice discounting contractual detail is complex but not central to the reported ratio.

notes: Merrill Lynch toilet fit-out appeal; rectification and project manager authority analysis is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Hurst v MLEP: rectification of construction final account settlement
key_facts: Hurst Stores fitted out toilet blocks at Merrill Lynch's London headquarters under a trade contract supervised by MLEP and construction manager Mace Ltd.
Hurst claimed about £6.5 million including disruption costs; MLEP relied on a document signed by Hurst's project manager Mr Mell on 27 April 2001 as full and final settlement of claims to that date.
The recorder granted declarations for rectification and that Mr Mell lacked authority to bind Hurst to the settlement wording.
Mr Mell understood the document only finalised CMI valuations for labour, plant and material and did not read the settlement clause on the last page.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from declarations granted by Mr Recorder Reese QC on rectification and authority in a construction payment dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; rectification upheld on unilateral mistake and shut-eye knowledge; Mr Mell lacked authority to agree a departure from the contractual valuation machinery.
enrichment.ratio: Rectification may be granted where the beneficiary knew or wilfully shut his eyes to the other's mistake as to settlement wording added without discussion; a project manager without express power cannot bind his employer to forego disruption claims outside the contract's certification process.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Mell was mistaken about the 27 April 2001 document
Whether Mace had actual or shut-eye knowledge of the mistake
Whether rectification on unilateral mistake was available under Commission for New Towns v Cooper
Whether Mr Mell had authority to agree full and final settlement of disruption claims
index_terms: Commission for New Towns v Cooper
linked_authorities: Commission for New Towns v Cooper [1995] Ch 259
Sharpe v San Paulo Railway Company (1873) LR 8 Ch App 597
Baden v Société Générale [1993] 1 WLR 509

confidence.notes: Outcome and legal reasoning on rectification and authority are fully articulated in Buxton LJ's judgment.

notes: Long heroin importation retrial appeals; conviction safety analysis exhaustive though factually dense.

enrichment.short_title: Tekin and Jisl heroin importation conviction appeals
key_facts: After a nearly 70-day retrial at the Old Bailey, Gungor Tekin and Jan Jisl were convicted of fraudulent evasion of prohibition on importing 139 packages of diamorphine with street value over £7 million.
Tekin was sentenced to 21 years with a confiscation order; Jisl to 14 years; co-defendant Konakli pleaded guilty and received 15 years.
The Crown case centred on surveillance, telephone traffic to Turkey, and a midnight meeting at Medway Travel Lodge where Jisl's minibus and Tekin's car converged.
Defence cases alleged set-up by informants and drug dealer Mentesh Hassan, with extensive cross-examination of Tekin over about 40 hours.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Criminal appeals against conviction with leave and renewed sentence application by Konakli following a lengthy retrial.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed; Konakli's sentence reduced from 15 to 13 years imprisonment for insufficient credit for guilty plea on retrial.
enrichment.ratio: Robust cross-examination and a lengthy summing up do not render convictions unsafe where the defendant remained in command of his evidence and specific criticisms of trial conduct lack cumulative prejudice; refusal to admit Aktolun's statement under ss 23 and 26 was a proper exercise of discretion.
legal_issues: Whether Tekin's cross-examination was oppressive and rendered convictions unsafe
Admissibility of Faruk Aktolun's statement under ss 23 and 26 of the 1988 Act
Whether the summing up was too long, inaudible or structurally unfair
Specific alleged errors in directions on Czech witnesses, observation evidence and lies
linked_authorities: R v Chaaban [2003] EWCA Crim 1012

confidence.notes: Appellate conclusions are clear though the underlying trial facts are exceptionally voluminous.

notes: Jemma Trust professional negligence trial; most claims dismissed with one narrow negligence finding upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Jemma Trust negligence claims against Kippax Beaumont Lewis
key_facts: Jemma Trust Company Ltd sued Kippax Beaumont Lewis (KBL), solicitors for executors of Sir Geoffrey Reynolds, in two linked professional negligence actions concerning estate and trust tax planning.
The disputes involved a deed of variation (DOV) and capital gains tax planning around assents and potential failed potentially exempt transfers by Lady Hulton.
KBL partners Mr Venables and Mr Marriott advised on complex IHT and CGT structures involving Reynolds family property and shareholdings.
The trial lasted 13 days with combined costs exceeding £1 million before trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of two Chancery professional negligence actions following lengthy pre-trial litigation.
enrichment.outcome: DOV action dismissed entirely; in the CGT action all negligence claims dismissed except paragraph 3.2B, where negligence was upheld and loss referred to enquiry.
enrichment.ratio: Executors' compromise with the Revenue and subsequent negotiations can negate loss caused by negligent tax advice; a solicitor may be negligent in failing to advise on PET/IHT exposure before assent yet claimants may fail to prove resulting financial loss on the facts.
legal_issues: Whether KBL negligently advised on deed of variation and Reynolds family negotiations
Whether negligence in CGT and IHT planning caused recoverable loss
Whether failed PET exposure was adequately advised before vesting assents
Causation of loss following Revenue compromise

confidence.notes: Final orders are clear but the tax planning fact pattern is intricate and most liability issues were dismissed.

notes: Simcyp software copyright appeal; Research Agreement clause 9 construction and agency analysis are central.

enrichment.short_title: Cyprotex v Sheffield: Simcyp software copyright ownership
key_facts: Cyprotex employed Dr Edwards to convert Sheffield University's MathCAD-based Simcyp pharmacokinetic models into commercial Java software under a multi-sponsor Research Agreement.
Sheffield claimed copyright in Java class libraries and GUI programs; Cyprotex claimed ownership as employer of the sole author absent contrary agreement.
The parties' commercial relationship broke down in 2001 before phase 2 completion, with competing exploitation claims.
Clause 9 of the Research Agreement allocated resulting intellectual property to the University subject to sponsor licences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from declaration that University of Sheffield owned copyright in Simcyp works created by Dr Edwards.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Sheffield's ownership declaration upheld on construction of the Research Agreement and Dr Edwards' role as university agent in performance of the programme.
enrichment.ratio: Work by a sponsor's programmer recruited to perform Sheffield's programme of research falls within clause 9(b) as work of an 'other agent' of the university; construing clause 9(d) to vest copyright in the sponsoring programmer would produce commercially unreal consequences inconsistent with the multipartite Research Agreement.
legal_issues: Ownership of copyright in software written by Dr Edwards
Construction of clause 9(a)-(d) of the Research Agreement
Whether Dr Edwards was agent of the university or sole employee of Cyprotex
Whether informal pre-agreement oral understandings affected IP allocation

linked_authorities: ICS v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

notes: Claygate restrictive covenant appeal; annexation under section 78 and user restriction construction clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Crest Nicholson v McAllister: Claygate covenant annexation
key_facts: Crest Nicholson sought declarations on restrictive covenants affecting Claygate, Surrey land it proposed to develop with six new houses on rear gardens and Redruth.
Mrs McAllister owned Newlyn, part of land conveyed in 1936 by Mitchell Brothers, and claimed benefit of covenants in earlier 1920s-1930s conveyances.
Covenants restricted use to private dwelling or professional purposes and required vendor approval for additional buildings.
The developer conceded there was no building scheme and McAllister could not enforce the 1936 Wing conveyance covenants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Neuberger J's declarations on construction and enforceability of historic restrictive covenants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; covenants in six earlier conveyances not enforceable by Mrs McAllister as annexation to her land failed; cross-appeal on spent building covenant not decided as academic.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 78 the land intended to be benefited must be defined so as to be easily ascertainable; express annexation for 'the part for the time being remaining unsold' excludes land subsequently sold off without express assignment, so a 1936 purchaser cannot enforce covenants imposed in earlier sales.
legal_issues: Whether benefit of covenants was annexed to Mrs McAllister's land under section 78
Effect of words annexing benefit to unsold parts of the Fee Farm Estate
Whether user covenant precludes more than one dwelling per plot
Whether building restriction became spent on death or dissolution of approving party

Marquess of Zetland v Driver [1939] Ch 1
Roake v Chadha [1984] 1 WLR 40
Rogers v Hosegood [1900] 2 Ch 388

notes: Pesticcio house gift undue influence appeal; Etridge and solicitor advice principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Niersmans v Pesticcio: undue influence over house gift
key_facts: Bernard Pesticcio, a vulnerable man with lifelong disabilities, gifted his Cardiff home to his sister Maureen Niersmans by deed dated 3 February 1998.
He had granted Maureen an enduring power of attorney and relied on her to manage his affairs after a serious fall and permanent nursing home residence from 1997.
Solicitor Dawn Tindall acted for Bernard in the gift, EPA and will but was found to have failed to give effective independent advice.
Maureen sold the house for £50,000 in 1999; Bernard's receiver later sued to set aside the gift.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Neuberger J's declaration that the 1998 deed of gift was procured by presumed undue influence and void.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; gift set aside; evidential burden on donee not rebutted despite solicitor involvement.
enrichment.ratio: Where trust and confidence and an unexplained substantial gift are proved, the evidential burden shifts to the donee; involvement of a solicitor does not automatically rebut presumed undue influence unless advice is relevant, effective and sufficient to free the donor's independent judgment.
legal_issues: Whether presumed undue influence arose from Bernard's trust in Maureen
Whether Miss Tindall's advice rebutted the presumption
Whether Maureen provided a satisfactory explanation for the gift
Appropriate remedy when solicitor advice was inadequate

notes: First section 49N national disqualification review appeal; scope of FHSAA review function authoritatively defined.

enrichment.short_title: Kataria appeal on NHS national disqualification review scope
key_facts: Dr Kataria was nationally disqualified by the NHS Tribunal in 1996 after findings of repeated failure to provide appropriate personal medical services and unreliable evidence.
The Family Health Services Appeal Authority dismissed his section 49N(7) review application in July 2003, assessing only post-1996 conduct.
Since disqualification he worked as a locum in Scotland and for the Armed Forces without disclosing the ban; the FHSAA criticised his failure to disclose and inadequate CPD.
This was the first High Court appeal from a section 49N review decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against FHSAA confirmation of national disqualification.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; FHSAA correctly held its review function was to assess whether disqualification should continue based on subsequent conduct, not to reconsider the original tribunal's findings.
enrichment.ratio: A section 49N(7) review is of the continuing national disqualification, not a rehearing of the original tribunal decision; minimum periods in section 49N(8) support finality, and the practitioner bears the onus of showing revocation would not prejudice NHS efficiency.
legal_issues: Scope of FHSAA review under section 49N(7)
Whether original NHS Tribunal findings could be reopened
Alleged bias and admission of witness statements without cross-examination
Whether disqualification confirmation was proportionate
linked_authorities: Rohatgi v Medical Tribunal of New South Wales [1998] 6 NSWCA Jud Rep
Madan v The GMC [2001] Lloyd's Rep Med 539
Chaudhury v The GMC (15 July 2002, unreported)

confidence.notes: First-instance High Court judgment comprehensively addresses scope of review and rejects all grounds of appeal.

notes: Public Munby judgment on intractable contact failure; systemic critique with clear factual findings on maternal obstruction.

enrichment.short_title: F v M: systemic failure in five-year contact dispute
key_facts: A father abandoned his five-year battle for contact with his seven-year-old daughter D after litigation from November 1998 involving 43 hearings before 16 judges.
Direct contact ceased in October 2001; the mother was imprisoned for breaching contact orders and repeatedly obstructed contact with groundless excuses.
The father was described by a clinical psychologist as a warm, caring parent with a secure attachment to his daughter.
Munby J published an anonymised public judgment criticising delay, lack of judicial continuity and failure to address parental alienation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Public High Court family judgment following private hearings in long-running residence and contact proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Father withdrew contact application; judgment documents systemic court failure and maternal implacable hostility without altering the practical outcome that contact had ended.
enrichment.ratio: Intractable contact disputes require judicial continuity, early fact-finding, swift enforcement and non-court dispute resolution; delay and failure to confront implacable hostility can irretrievably damage parent-child relationships and breach Article 8 rights to mutual enjoyment of family life.
legal_issues: Causes of failure in intractable contact litigation
Parental alienation and implacable hostility
Judicial case management and timetabling in private law cases
Article 8 and state obligation to facilitate contact

notes: Coflexip offshore pipe-laying patent appeal; validity and infringement restored on all points.

enrichment.short_title: Coflexip v Rockwater: offshore pipe-laying patent validity
key_facts: Coflexip (patentee) appealed against findings invalidating European Patent UK 0478742 relating to laying flexible offshore pipes.
Key claims covered a method (claim 1) and device (claim 3) for controlled pipe laying from a vessel.
Laddie J had held Rockwater's device did not infringe claim 3 and the patent was invalid for anticipation and obviousness.
The Court of Appeal previously gave conflicting judgments on claim 3 construction in 1999.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Laddie J's revocation and non-infringement judgment in patent proceedings brought by Rockwater Ltd.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on all points; patent held valid and infringed by Rockwater's device.
enrichment.ratio: On proper construction claim 3 is not invalid for anticipation or obviousness; the judge erred in treating prior winch disclosures and abandonment-and-recovery concepts as anticipating the claimed laying method and apparatus without regard to necessary modifications.
legal_issues: Construction of method claim 1 and device claim 3
Validity for anticipation and obviousness
Whether Rockwater's laying system infringed
Proper approach to abandonment and recovery prior art

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal unanimously allows appeal; detailed technical prior art analysis but clear ultimate holdings.
